newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: MALAYSIAN TEAM SAID TO BE HEADING FOR FOKKER TALKS.
newsitem.headline: MALAYSIAN TEAM SAID TO BE HEADING FOR FOKKER TALKS.

text.p: A four-strong team from the Malaysian government investment company Khazanah will visit the Netherlands on Wednesday to discuss a possible relaunch of bankrupt Dutch aircraft maker Fokker NV , the Dutch news agency ANP reported on Tuesday.

The agency based its report on remarks by a Dutch businessman based in Kuala Lumpur who it described as an intermediary between potential Dutch and Malaysian investors interested in backing a last-gasp rescue plan for Fokker.
In Amsterdam the court-appointed insolvency lawyers who have been running Fokker since it was declared bankrupt a year ago declined to make any comment on the report.
Earlier this month, however, they said talks would be held with Khazanah with a view to completing a rescue plan by May 1.
This followed an agreement between the Dutch parties involved in rescue talks on a common position for negotiations with the Malaysians.
That agreement was signed by the lawyers, the Dutch government, engineering firm Stork and Deleye Investment, a firm headed by Andre Deleye, chairman of Dutch industrial investment company Begemann .
The "Malaysian option" is seen as the final lifeline for Fokker, one of the pioneering companies of European aviation.
ANP said the Khazanah delegation would visit the Fokker assembly facilities near Amsterdam and would examine the company's books in a visit expected to last until Sunday.
It said tentative rescue plans assumed the Malaysians would invest 450 million guilders in a new Fokker, the Dutch state 475 million, Stork 175 million and Deleye 25 million.
Dutch Minister of Economic Affairs Hans Wijers warned against over-optimism a fortnight ago, saying there would be no relaunch unless substantial foreign investment could be secured.
Fokker was forced into bankruptcy last year when majority shareholder Daimler Benz AG of Germany pulled the plug, saying it could no longer bear Fokker's huge losses.
Malaysia's emergence as a potential saviour comes after a number of suitors -- from Canadians and South Koreans to Russians -- failed to come up with a viable rescue package.
Insolvency lawyers have kept Fokker's factory near Amsterdam working on a handful of outstanding orders, but most of the company's skilled labour force has long since left.
Unless the Malaysian option goes ahead the plant is expected to be closed for good this summer and the assets liquidated.
After Daimler abandoned Fokker, Stork bought the profitable Fokker aircraft maintenance and components businesses in a deal binding it to involvement in a relaunch.
Industry sources say a Fokker relaunch would face massive start-up costs and take up to a year to get off the ground.
